42911850.text: Several congenital, traumatic, infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic processes, as well as iatrogenic interventions, can alter intraluminal contents of the pancreatic duct, leading to adverse outcomes. Variant ductal anatomy may result in clinically significant complications such as duodenal obstruction, acute and chronic pancreatitis, and increased risk of developing gallbladder or biliary malignancies. The presence of calculi, blood, pus, and other unintended iatrogenic material in the pancreatic duct can be associated with a range of complications. Neoplastic involvement of the pancreatic duct by entities other than ductal adenocarcinoma is uncommon but may occur secondary to tumor extension into the duct or de novo development. CT and MRI or MR cholangiopancreatography are the most commonly used imaging modalities for evaluating the pancreatic duct and associated pathologic processes. Endoscopic US and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography are more invasive imaging options that also provide the option of simultaneous intervention, if needed. The authors include discussion of the imaging appearances of various congenital anomalies and pathologic processes of the pancreatic duct and complications of ductal disruption and abnormal intraluminal contents. The section on neoplasia provides an up-to-date review of imaging manifestations of recently described neoplastic entities that develop within the pancreatic duct. Awareness of these abnormalities and their imaging correlates may help radiologists improve patient care.

42912550.text: Gastric metastases from neuroendocrine tumors (NET) are infrequently encountered. Commonly, locally advanced pancreatic NET can involve stomach resulting in inoperable presentation. We herein present a case of gastric wall metastatic disease in postoperative pancreatic NET, which was identified on [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE-PET/CT as recurrence of disease after prolong progression-free period. [18F]F-FDG avidity of the lesions on [18F]F-FDG-PET/CT indicated requirement of chemotherapy alone, or in combination with [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). Hence, dual-tracer PET/CT imaging proved important in identifying unusual metastatic disease site and deciding therapeutic strategies in GEP-NET after a long follow-up period following surgical removal of primary disease.

42972950.label: Objectives
42972950.text: Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) are routinely used to enhance magnetic resonance (MR) imaging. In recent years, GBCA residues were detected in multiple organs, with the kidney as the primary organ of excretion showing the highest concentrations. This study aimed to map the intricate spatial distribution of GBCA residues in rat kidneys at an early and a late time point.

42972950.label: Materials and methods
42972950.text: Rats received one of 6 marketed GBCAs [3 macrocyclic, 3 linear; cumulative dose 4.8 mmol gadolinium (Gd)/kg] or saline and were sacrificed at day 5 or week 14 post administration (n = 5 per GBCA and time point). In whole renal tissue slices, the distribution of elemental Gd was determined by laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry and the distribution of intact GBCA chelates by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-mass spectrometry imaging. In ex vivo kidneys, MR relaxometry was used to assess MR-detectable GBCA residues.

42972950.label: Results
42972950.text: At day 5, Gd was predominantly localized in the renal cortex across all GBCAs, with 10- to 100-fold lower medullary levels. Distribution patterns corresponded well with those of exemplary intact GBCA chelates. At week 14, Gd levels had decreased by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude. Distribution patterns from linear GBCAs showed Gd remaining predominantly in the cortex, while Gd from macrocyclic GBCAs was similar in cortex and medulla. Several GBCAs exhibited a prominent Gd presence at the transition zone between outer and inner medulla. Intact chelate was only detectable for the exemplary macrocyclic GBCA, with a spatial distribution pattern matching that of elemental Gd. MR relaxometry detected GBCA residues within ex vivo kidneys but also in the surrounding water-based fixative. This indicated the presence and washout of intact GBCAs, which was greater for macrocyclic versus linear GBCAs.

42972950.label: Conclusions
42972950.text: This study provides the first comprehensive spatially resolved characterization of renal GBCA residues at an early and a late time point. GBCA residues exhibited specific intrarenal distribution patterns and distinct changes in these patterns over the course of their elimination. Our findings of specific retention patterns suggest that renal microanatomy and local physicochemical conditions play critical roles in GBCA retention. These insights provide a foundation for future investigations into retention mechanisms and potential long-term tissue effects.
